summary.text: At $n=1$, the defining sum has only its $k=0$ term, giving $a(1)=8/(2)=4$. Since $1=2^0$ but $4$ is even, this is a counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\beta(k)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}^{2}\binom{k+j}{j},
\]
and let \(t(k)\) be the coefficient of \(x^k\) in \((x^2+4x-1)^k\). Equivalently,
\[
t(k)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}(-1)^i
\binom{k}{i}\binom{k-i}{i}4^{k-2i}.
\]
For every positive integer \(n\), the sequence in the conjecture is defined by
\[
a(n)=\frac1{2n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k(15k+8)\beta(k)t(k).
\]

We disprove the asserted parity characterization by taking \(n=1\).

First,
\[
\beta(0)=\sum_{j=0}^{0}\binom{0}{j}^{2}\binom{0+j}{j}
=\binom00^2\binom00=1.
\]
Also, \((x^2+4x-1)^0=1\), so the coefficient of \(x^0\) is
\[
t(0)=1.
\]
The same value follows directly from the displayed finite-sum formula: its sole term is
\[
(-1)^0\binom00\binom00 4^0=1.
\]

The sum defining \(a(1)\) contains only the term \(k=0\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(1)
&=\frac1{2\cdot1}(-1)^0(15\cdot0+8)\beta(0)t(0)\\
&=\frac12\cdot1\cdot8\cdot1\cdot1\\
&=4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(a(1)\) is indeed an integer, but it is even, not odd.

On the other hand, \(1\) is a positive power of two, since
\[
1=2^0.
\]
Consequently, at the positive integer \(n=1\), the statement “\(n\) is a power of two” is true while the statement “\(a(n)\) is odd” is false. Hence the claimed equivalence
\[
a(n)\text{ is odd}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\text{ is a power of two}
\]
fails for \(n=1\). Since the conjecture asserts the conjunction of integrality and this equivalence for every \(n>0\), failure of the equivalence at this single positive integer disproves the entire conjecture.
